gap: No result ChatGPT got states that under $20 the 'watts' on the box mean three different things. Anker's $15.99 Nano Charger Neo (A120M) is sold as 45W but its maker says it gives up to 65 W and starts cutting power after about 20 minutes at 65 W. UGREEN's 45W Nexode Air does PPS only up to 11 V, and the $15.99 Nano 30W (A2147) only up to 16 V. Samsung's 60 W mode needs 20 V/3 A over PPS and iPhone 18 Pro's top speed needs a 60 W AVS charger, so the 30W pick ChatGPT gave meets neither.
standout_why: Compared against the two cited pages and Android Authority's list. TechGearLab's Anker Nano 30W review gives 29.4 W measured and says the charger is not the best for iPhone 18 Pro, but it gives no PPS range and does not mention AVS. Android Authority (cited in chat 2, dated 2025-11-27) says the Nano 3 30W gives 27 W over PPS and 'cannot supply the 20V some PPS phones need'. That is part of the finding, and it covers only that one charger: the page does not list the Nano Charger Neo, the Nexode Air 45W or the UGREEN Uno, and it only mentions AVS in passing for iPhone 17. Tom's Hardware's best-chargers page (cited) would not load past its headline, so I could not check it; that is why this is a 2 and not a 3. None of the pages I could read explains the Neo's 45W-vs-65W label or how long the 65 W lasts.
decides: This moves the top pick away from the Nano 30W for iPhone 18 Pro owners and confirms it is no worse for Samsung. At the same $15.99 on anker.com today, the Nano Charger Neo is the only candidate whose maker states both 65 W and AVS. The Nano 30W's maker page lists 20 V/1.5 A on PD and a PPS ceiling of 16 V, and does not mention AVS. Apple asks for a 60W-capable AVS adapter on USB-PD 3.2. Two limits on the Neo: its AVS support comes only from Anker's FAQ and has not been tested independently, and Anker says it starts lowering its 65 W after about 20 minutes. For Samsung, no charger here is published as giving 20 V over PPS (the Neo's range is not published at all). So the S26 Ultra's 60 W / about 48 W mode cannot be promised under $20, and the Nexode Air 45W's 5–11 V at 4.5 A PPS covers the 45 W class at most (a reviewer's expectation, not a measurement). None of the chargers Dealectric links is under $20. The page's own-row rule probably triggers a skip unless the UGREEN Nexode Air 45W gets a record at a price read and confirmed under $20.

findings.label: Price, anker.com US
findings.source_title: Anker Nano Charger Neo - Anker US
findings.note: Black Friday price. The page gives no sale end date. Anker's page lists the features as 'Dynamic 45W - 65W Fast Charging'.

findings.label: What the '45W' in the name means
findings.value: Up to 65 W maximum output. Anker says the 45W 'refers to the charging capability of specific devices'
findings.source_title: Why does the charger's product name list 45W when the charger supports up to 65W output? (A120M) - Anker Support
findings.note: Maker's own statement. The 45W in the name is not a guaranteed output, and 65 W is the peak.

findings.label: How long it holds 65 W
findings.value: Starts lowering its power after about 20 minutes at 65 W
findings.source_title: How is A120M 65W Power Derating Duration? (A120M) - Anker Support
findings.note: Anker calls this normal thermal protection. The timing depends on room temperature, the device and its battery level. Anker does not say what wattage it drops to.

findings.label: Phone fast-charge modes (maker)
findings.value: AVS and PPS, up to 65 W
findings.source_title: What are the differences between A120M and A121D? (A120M) - Anker Support
findings.note: Anker's spec page (service.anker.com/product-description/a08e200000XNcEWAA1) lists the protocols as 'PD3.1\PPS\PPS\AFC\FCP\SCP\UFCS', a 65W maximum, one USB-C port and a size of 34×36.5×43.2 mm. It does not list AVS or PPS voltage ranges. AVS is stated only in this FAQ.

findings.label: Measured laptop draw (named reviewer)
findings.value: 59.8 W live draw; 65 W profile negotiated with a 5 A cable, 60 W with a 3 A cable
findings.source_title: Anker Nano Charger Neo - The Gadgeteer (Rei Padla, updated 2026-11-04)
findings.note: Tested on a MacBook Air M5 using macOS's power readings, not an external meter. USB PD 3.0 was negotiated and AVS was not, which is expected because a Mac does not request AVS. The reviewer did not verify how long it sustains output.

findings.label: PD fixed profiles
findings.note: Spec table in the review. 20 V × 2.25 A = 45 W.

findings.label: PPS range
findings.note: 11 V × 4.5 A = 49.5 W ceiling. The reviewer expects 40–45 W on PPS phones, including Samsung; this is not a measurement. For comparison, the review gives the Nexode Air 65W 5–11 V at 5 A plus 5–21 V at 3.25 A. The review also says both models support SPR AVS. UGREEN's spec sheet and ChargerLAB do not confirm that, and Charge-Test found AVS missing on a 'Version 1' Nexode Air 65W, so the 45W's AVS may depend on hardware version.

findings.label: PD and PPS output (maker)
findings.value: PD 5V⎓3A, 9V⎓3A, 15V⎓2A, 20V⎓1.5A; PPS 3.3–11V⎓3A and 3.3–16V⎓2A (30 W max); AVS not listed
findings.note: The PPS ceiling of 16 V rules out Samsung's 20 V/3 A PPS mode. Android Authority measured 27 W over PPS and 89.3% efficiency (androidauthority.com/best-usb-c-wall-chargers-3496950).

findings.label: Measured single-port output
findings.value: 29.4 W; iPhone 17 Pro from 10% to 60% in 29 minutes
findings.source_title: Anker Nano 30W Review | Tested & Rated - TechGearLab
findings.note: The reviewer calls it 'not the best charger for the iPhone 18 Pro and above'.

findings.label: What iPhone 18 Pro needs for top wired speed
findings.value: A 60W-capable (or greater) adapter with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) that supports USB-PD 3.2
findings.source_title: Fast charge your iPhone - Apple Support
findings.note: Apple's testing footnote on the same page says 'USB PD 3.1 (or better) ... with AVS'. The page does not say what a 20 W or 30 W adapter gives an 18 Pro.

findings.label: What Galaxy S26 Ultra needs for its 60 W mode
findings.value: A USB PD 3.1 charger with PPS at 20 V/3 A from one port. 60 W lasts about 2 minutes, then about 48 W holds for about 16 minutes
findings.source_title: I tested the Galaxy S26 Ultra's 60W charging - Android Authority (Robert Triggs, 2026-04-06)
findings.note: The article says 'the 20V requirement is not so common'. Of the under-$20 chargers here, the Nano 30W's maker range stops at 16 V and the Nexode Air 45W's reviewed range at 11 V, so neither reaches this mode.
